Front: Explain `Access modifier:` deeply enough for review.
Back: A keyword (public, protected, private) or default package-private access that regulates the visibility of classes, interfaces, constructors, methods, and fields.
Extra: In Java, access control is enforced at compile-time. If you try to access a private field from outside its declaring class, or a default field from another package, it fails with a compile error.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Access modifier:`?
Back: Do not confuse visibility (who can see/use the member) with other properties like accessibility via reflection, or static vs instance behavior.
Extra: Standard access modifiers only apply to compile-time access rules. Reflection (setAccessible(true)) can bypass them at runtime unless a SecurityManager/JVM module restrictions prevent it.

Front: Explain `public` deeply enough for review.
Back: public allows unrestricted access from any other class in any package, provided the containing class is also visible.
Extra: Example: `public class Logger { public void log(String msg) { ... } }`. If the class itself is package-private (default), declaring a method as public does not make it visible outside that package.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `public`?
Back: Do not confuse public visibility of a member with the visibility of the class containing it.
Extra: If class `A` is default (package-private) in package `p1`, a `public` method inside `A` cannot be called from package `p2` because class `A` itself is inaccessible.

Front: Explain `protected` deeply enough for review.
Back: protected allows access from classes in the same package and subclasses in any package.
Extra: When accessed by a subclass in another package, it can ONLY be accessed through references of that subclass type or its sub-types, not through a reference of the parent class.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `protected`?
Back: A subclass in package `p2` cannot access a `protected` member of a superclass in package `p1` using a parent class reference.
Extra: `package p2; public class Child extends Parent { void test() { x = 1; // OK\nParent p = new Parent(); p.x = 2; // COMPILE ERROR } }`
Code: package p1; public class Parent { protected int x; }

Front: Explain `default` deeply enough for review.
Back: default access (package-private, no keyword) restricts visibility to classes residing in the same package.
Extra: There is no `default` keyword for access control (the `default` keyword is used in switch statements, interface default methods, or annotations). Lack of modifier means package-private.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `default`?
Back: Do not try to write the word `default` as an access modifier.
Extra: Writing `default void myMethod() {}` inside a normal class is a compile-time error. It is only valid as an interface method modifier to provide a default implementation.

Front: Explain `private` deeply enough for review.
Back: private restricts member visibility to the declaring top-level class only.
Extra: Nested classes can access private members of their outer class, and vice-versa, because they belong to the same top-level class. Since Java 11, nested nestmates share access natively.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `private`?
Back: private members are not inherited by subclasses, but they are still present in the subclass object memory layout.
Extra: Although a subclass inherits all visible fields/methods, it does not inherit private fields. However, if the superclass has public getters/setters, the subclass can modify the private state.

Front: Explain `Non-access modifier:` deeply enough for review.
Back: Keywords that modify the behavior of classes, methods, or variables without altering their visibility/access levels.
Extra: Common examples include static (class-level), final (non-overridable), abstract (incomplete), synchronized (locking/thread safety), and volatile (thread visibility). They do not restrict who can access the member, only how it behaves.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Non-access modifier:`?
Back: Do not assume non-access modifiers cannot be combined.
Extra: You can combine them (e.g., `public static final int MAX = 10;` or `protected synchronized static void run() {}`). However, some combinations like `abstract final` or `abstract static` are illegal.

Front: Explain `static` deeply enough for review.
Back: static associates a member (field or method) with the class itself rather than with instances of the class.
Extra: There is only one copy of a static variable per JVM ClassLoader. Static methods cannot access instance variables (`this` or `super` cannot be used).

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `static`?
Back: Do not think static methods participate in runtime polymorphic overriding.
Extra: If a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a superclass static method, it is hidden, not overridden. The method called depends on the reference type, not the runtime object.

Front: Explain `final` deeply enough for review.
Back: final prevents reassignment of variables, overriding of methods, or subclassing of classes.
Extra: A final variable can only be assigned once. A final class cannot be extended. A final method cannot be overridden by subclasses.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `final`?
Back: Making a reference variable final makes the reference immutable, but the referenced object's internal state can still change.
Extra:
Code example:
`final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add('hello'); // OK! Internal state can change
list = new ArrayList<>(); // Compile error! Cannot reassign reference`

Front: Explain `abstract` deeply enough for review.
Back: abstract marks a class or method as incomplete, meaning it cannot be instantiated and must be completed by concrete subclasses.
Extra: An abstract class can have instance variables, concrete methods, and constructors (which are called by subclass constructors), whereas interfaces focus on behavioral contracts.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `abstract`?
Back: Do not declare abstract methods inside a non-abstract class, or combine abstract with final/private.
Extra: Any class containing at least one abstract method MUST be declared abstract. Also, abstract methods cannot be private or final because subclasses must be able to override them.

Front: Explain `synchronized` deeply enough for review.
Back: synchronized ensures that only one thread can execute a block of code or method at a time by acquiring a monitor lock.
Extra: An instance synchronized method locks on the `this` object. A static synchronized method locks on the `Class` object associated with the declaring class.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `synchronized`?
Back: Do not assume synchronized automatically provides atomic operations for all variables, or that threads cannot access non-synchronized methods.
Extra: A thread can freely call other non-synchronized methods on the same object even if another thread holds the lock for a synchronized method on that object.

Front: Explain `volatile` deeply enough for review.
Back: volatile guarantees that reads/writes of a variable are directly made to main memory, ensuring thread visibility.
Extra: It prevents the JVM and CPU from caching variables or reordering instructions around it, but it does NOT guarantee atomicity for compound operations (like `count++`).

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `volatile`?
Back: volatile is not a replacement for synchronized; it does not protect critical sections or make compound operations atomic.
Extra: For example, `volatile int count = 0; count++;` is NOT thread-safe. `count++` is a read-modify-write operation. Use `synchronized` or `AtomicInteger` for atomicity.

Front: Explain `transient` deeply enough for review.
Back: transient prevents a field from being serialized when using Java's built-in serialization mechanism.
Extra: When the object is deserialized, transient fields are initialized to their default values (e.g., `null` for objects, `0` for numbers, `false` for booleans).

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `transient`?
Back: Static fields are not serialized either, but they are not transient.
Extra: Static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so Java serialization ignores them by default. Making a static field transient is redundant and has no effect on serialization.

Front: Explain `native` deeply enough for review.
Back: native indicates that a method is implemented in another language (like C or C++) using the Java Native Interface (JNI).
Extra: A native method has no body, just a semicolon at the end of its signature: `public native void fastCopy();`. It cannot be declared abstract.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `native`?
Back: Do not put a method body (even empty braces) for a native method declaration.
Extra: Writing `public native void doSomething() {}` will cause a compile-time error. A native method's declaration must end with a semicolon, exactly like an abstract method.

Front: Explain `strictfp` deeply enough for review.
Back: strictfp ensures floating-point calculations are consistently executed across platforms using the IEEE 754 standard.
Extra: Since Java 17, all floating-point operations in Java are strict by default. Therefore, the strictfp keyword has become completely obsolete and redundant, though it is still accepted for backward compatibility.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `strictfp`?
Back: strictfp is obsolete starting with Java 17.
Extra: Although it is still a reserved keyword and compiles, it has no effect in modern Java because strict IEEE 754 compliance is now standard.

Front: Explain `Static variable` deeply enough for review.
Back: A variable declared with the static modifier, sharing a single value across all instances of a class.
Extra: Static variables are stored in the Metaspace (part of native memory) from Java 8 onwards (previously in the PermGen heap). They are initialized when the class is loaded.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Static variable`?
Back: Do not access static variables through object instances, even though Java allows it.
Extra: Writing `myObj.staticVar` will compile but is bad practice. The compiler replaces it with `MyClass.staticVar`. If `myObj` is null, `myObj.staticVar` still works without throwing a NullPointerException!

Front: Explain `Static method` deeply enough for review.
Back: A method declared with the static modifier that belongs to the class and can be invoked without creating an instance.
Extra: Static methods can only access other static members of their class directly. They cannot reference `this` or `super` because they are not executed within an object context.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Static method`?
Back: Static methods cannot be overridden by subclasses in a polymorphic way.
Extra: If a subclass defines a static method with the exact same signature, it only hides the parent method. Which method executes depends on the compile-time type of the reference.

Front: Explain `Static block` deeply enough for review.
Back: A static block is a code block inside a class that runs once when the class is first loaded into memory.
Extra: It is typically used for complex initialization of static variables. Multiple static blocks run in the order they appear in the source file.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Static block`?
Back: Do not assume static blocks run when an object is created; they run once during class loading, before any constructor.
Extra: If a class is loaded but never instantiated, its static blocks still execute. Static blocks cannot throw checked exceptions unless they are caught within the block.

Front: Explain `Static nested class` deeply enough for review.
Back: A nested class declared static, which does not hold an implicit reference to an instance of the outer class.
Extra: It can be instantiated without an instance of the outer class: `Outer.StaticNested nested = new Outer.StaticNested();`. It can only access outer class's static members.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Static nested class`?
Back: Do not confuse it with an inner class (non-static nested class).
Extra: Non-static inner classes require an outer instance to be instantiated and hold an implicit reference to it. Static nested classes do not, saving memory and avoiding potential memory leaks.

Front: Explain `Static import` deeply enough for review.
Back: A feature that allows static members (fields and methods) to be accessed without class qualification.
Extra: Example: `import static java.lang.Math.PI;` allows using `double r = PI * 2;` directly instead of `Math.PI * 2`.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Static import`?
Back: Do not overuse static imports or confuse `import static` syntax with normal static declarations.
Extra: Overusing static imports can make code unreadable by polluting the namespace. The syntax must be `import static package.Class.Member;` (not `static import`).

Front: Explain `Final variable` deeply enough for review.
Back: A variable whose value cannot be reassigned once initialized.
Extra: For primitives, the value is constant. For objects, the reference is constant, but the object's properties can still be modified.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Final variable`?
Back: Do not think a final object reference guarantees immutability of the object itself.
Extra: If `final Person p = new Person();`, you cannot do `p = new Person();`, but you can do `p.setName('Bob');`. To make the object immutable, the class itself must be designed to be immutable.

Front: Explain `Final method` deeply enough for review.
Back: A method that cannot be overridden or hidden by any subclass.
Extra: Methods called from constructors should generally be final to prevent subclasses from executing code on an uninitialized subclass state.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Final method`?
Back: Private methods are implicitly final in Java, so adding final to them is redundant.
Extra: Since a private method cannot be seen or overridden by subclasses anyway, marking it final is unnecessary, though the compiler allows it.

Front: Explain `Final class` deeply enough for review.
Back: A class that cannot be extended (subclassed) by any other class.
Extra: Making a class final prevents the creation of subclasses, ensuring that its implementation cannot be altered or broken through inheritance (e.g., `java.lang.String`).

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Final class`?
Back: Final classes are not automatically immutable; their fields can still be modified unless the fields themselves are final.
Extra: Marking a class final only prevents subclassing. If the class has public/package-private mutable fields, those fields can still be changed.

Front: Explain `Final parameter` deeply enough for review.
Back: A method or constructor parameter whose value cannot be reassigned within the method body.
Extra: It prevents accidental modification of parameter values inside the method. It is also required for local variables/parameters accessed by anonymous inner classes or lambda expressions prior to Java 8 (which introduced 'effectively final').

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Final parameter`?
Back: Marking a parameter final does not prevent changes to the state of the object passed.
Extra: If a method signature is `void log(final List<String> list)`, you cannot assign `list = null;` inside the method, but you can do `list.add('log');`.

Front: Explain `Blank final variable` deeply enough for review.
Back: A final variable that is declared without an initial value.
Extra: A blank final instance variable must be initialized in every constructor of the class. A blank final static variable must be initialized in a static initializer block.

Front: What confusion should you avoid with `Blank final variable`?
Back: Failing to initialize a blank final variable in all constructor paths causes a compile-time error.
Extra: The compiler performs definite assignment analysis. If there is even one path in a constructor where a blank final instance variable is not assigned, the code will fail to compile.
